source: Meridian Assurance Group (fictional) principle catalogs: laptop sample library

principles.name: Primacy of Principles
principles.statement: These principles apply to every part of Meridian Assurance Group, to every line of business, and to every initiative that changes the enterprise — whether delivered internally, by a partner, or bought as a service.
principles.rationale: Meridian's federated operating model has historically allowed each line of business to procure and deploy systems with little central review. The result is four customer masters, sixty point-to-point interfaces and a landscape nobody owns. A principle set that applies only where it is convenient does not constrain anything and will not correct that pattern. Consistent application is also what makes architecture compliance assessable, and therefore what makes the Joint Standard 1 of 2023 IT governance obligation demonstrable rather than asserted.
principles.implications:
1. Every initiative that creates, changes or retires a business capability, an application, a data store or a technology component is subject to architecture compliance review.
2. Vendor-delivered and SaaS solutions are assessed against these principles on the same terms as internal builds. Procurement must include architecture review before contract signature.
3. Where a principle cannot be met, the route is a recorded dispensation under GP-02, not silent non-compliance.
4. The Architecture Board requires the authority to withhold approval. Without it this principle is decorative.
principles.measure: Percentage of initiatives above the materiality threshold that passed through architecture review before funding approval. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Maximise Benefit to the Enterprise
principles.statement: Architecture decisions are made to deliver maximum long-term benefit to Meridian as a whole, even where this is not the fastest or cheapest option for an individual line of business.
principles.rationale: Each line of business carries its own profit and loss, which correctly drives local optimisation. Applied to shared assets — customer data, integration, product configuration, the technology estate — local optimisation has produced duplicated capability and an estate whose run cost consumes 71% of the technology budget. The Meridian 2030 targets of a single customer view and a cost-to-income ratio below 32% cannot be met by four separately optimised businesses.
principles.implications:
1. Some initiatives will be slower or more expensive for a single line of business than a local solution would have been. That cost must be visible and consciously accepted, not hidden.
2. A funding and chargeback model is required for shared capability, or no line of business will pay for it.
3. Line-of-business managing directors must be represented on the Architecture Board so that enterprise decisions are made with them rather than to them.
4. Priorities must be established and changed only at the enterprise level; component-level priority setting reintroduces the problem.
principles.measure: Duplicate capability instances across lines of business, by capability. Trend must be downward each ADM cycle.

principles.name: Fair Customer Outcomes by Design
principles.statement: Business processes and the systems that support them are designed so that fair customer outcomes are produced by default and can be evidenced from data, not asserted after the fact.
principles.rationale: The COFI Bill moves South African conduct regulation from prescriptive rules to an outcomes-based framework centred on fair treatment across the value chain. An outcomes regime cannot be satisfied by a compliance function reviewing samples; it requires the enterprise to show, from its own records, what happened to a customer across advice, sale, servicing and claim. Meridian cannot presently assemble that view because the advice record, the policy record and the claim record share no key.
principles.implications:
1. Every customer-affecting process must emit an auditable event to a common customer timeline, keyed to a single customer identifier.
2. Conduct outcome measures must be defined as data — not as manual attestations — and must be reportable without a project.
3. Product design must consider the outcome for the least sophisticated customer in the target market, not the average one.
4. This principle will sometimes slow a product launch. It takes precedence over speed to market.
principles.measure: Proportion of active policyholders for whom a complete advice-to-claim timeline can be produced from systems of record within one working day. Target: 100% by 2030.

principles.name: Business Continuity
principles.statement: Enterprise operations continue in spite of interruption to any single system, site, supplier or utility. Continuity requirements are stated as business outcomes, not as technology configurations.
principles.rationale: Meridian operates in an environment of continued grid unreliability, and holds regulated obligations to policyholders that do not pause when a data centre, a branch or a supplier fails. Joint Standard 2 of 2024 requires demonstrable cyber resilience. Designing for continuity after the fact is materially more expensive than designing for it at the outset, and concentration risk in the legacy life platform is already a stated concern of the Chief Risk Officer.
principles.implications:
1. Recovery time and recovery point objectives must be set by the business owner of each capability, and must be tested rather than documented.
2. Single points of failure — including single suppliers and single skilled individuals — must be recorded on the risk register with a named mitigation.
3. Resilience is designed proportionately (see TP-04); not every capability warrants the same investment.
4. Dependencies on external parties, including the bancassurance partner, must be covered by tested contingency arrangements.
principles.measure: Percentage of capabilities rated Critical with an RTO/RPO tested within the last 12 months. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Compliance is Designed, Not Retrofitted
principles.statement: Regulatory and statutory obligations are treated as architecture requirements from the outset of a change, with the evidence they demand designed into the solution.
principles.rationale: Meridian's obligations under COFI, IFRS 17, POPIA, FAIS, FICA and the Joint Standards are not periodic reporting exercises; each requires evidence generated by day-to-day operations. Regulators have moved into a higher enforcement gear, demanding demonstrable results rather than compliance on paper, and the FSCA has shown willingness to sanction individual executives as well as firms. Retrofitting evidence is the most expensive way to obtain it and the least reliable.
principles.implications:
1. The compliance function must be a participant in architecture work, not a reviewer at the end of it.
2. Every architecture requirement traceable to a regulatory obligation must be tagged as such in the Requirements Repository so its cost of removal is visible.
3. Regulatory horizon scanning feeds Phase H; a new obligation is an architecture change request, not only a compliance project.
4. Where an obligation's interpretation is uncertain, the architecture must preserve optionality rather than assume the most convenient reading.
principles.measure: Proportion of regulatory obligations mapped to a named architecture requirement and an owning capability. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Change is Incremental and Reversible
principles.statement: The enterprise changes through sequenced increments that each deliver stated business value and each leave the organisation in a stable, operable state. Large irreversible transitions are avoided.
principles.rationale: Two core-replacement attempts, in 2016 and 2021, were framed as technology programmes, proceeded without an agreed target architecture and were unwound at significant cost. The organisation's appetite for a third big-bang is exhausted, and its confidence must be rebuilt through delivery rather than argument. Incremental change also allows the roadmap to absorb regulatory change without restarting.
principles.implications:
1. Every roadmap must be expressed as work packages and transition architectures, each with a defined value contribution and a stable end state.
2. A transition state that cannot be operated in production is not a transition architecture; it is a partially completed project.
3. Coexistence of old and new is expected and must be designed for, including data synchronisation and reconciliation during the overlap.
4. This principle constrains ambition per increment. It does not lower the target.
principles.measure: Proportion of approved work packages that deliver a stable, operable transition state within two quarters. Target: 90%.

principles.name: Data is a Shared Enterprise Asset
principles.statement: Data is an asset of Meridian as a whole, not of the line of business, system or project that captured it, and is made available for any legitimate enterprise purpose consistent with the terms on which it was collected.
principles.rationale: Meridian's most valuable data — who its customers are, what they hold, what they have claimed — is fragmented across four customer masters and a set of departmental marts. Treating data as project property is what produced that state. Wide, governed access improves the speed and quality of decisions and removes the manual matching effort currently applied to roughly 640,000 records.
principles.implications:
1. No system may treat data it holds as private to itself; interfaces for legitimate enterprise access must be provided.
2. Sharing is governed, not unconditional. Access is granted against a stated purpose consistent with the POPIA basis on which the data was collected (see DP-04).
3. An education effort is required so that business units understand the relationship between the value of data, the sharing of data and access to it.
4. Data supplied to the enterprise must be of sufficient quality for others to rely on; the cost of quality falls on the producer, not the consumer.
principles.measure: Proportion of enterprise-significant data entities registered in the data catalogue with a documented access route. Target: 100% of Tier 1 entities.

principles.name: One Authoritative Source per Data Entity
principles.statement: Each enterprise data entity has exactly one designated authoritative source. All other holdings are copies, are identified as such, and are never used as the basis for a decision that the authoritative source could answer.
principles.rationale: Four customer masters produce four answers to the question of who a customer is, and no basis for choosing between them. This directly obstructs the single customer view, COFI outcome evidence, FICA due diligence and IFRS 17 contract-level reporting simultaneously. Designating an authoritative source is the smallest change that makes all four tractable, and it must precede any attempt to consolidate the underlying systems.
principles.implications:
1. Customer, party, product, policy, claim and adviser must each be assigned an authoritative source and a single enterprise identifier scheme.
2. Copies are permitted for performance and resilience, but must be traceable to the authority and must carry the currency of the data they hold.
3. Designating the authority is a business decision made by the data owner, not a technical decision made by a project.
4. Legacy systems that cannot surrender authority must be wrapped so that the authority is exposed through a managed interface (see AP-02).
principles.measure: Number of enterprise data entities with more than one system claiming authority. Target: zero for Tier 1 entities by 2028.

principles.name: Data is Owned and Stewarded
principles.statement: Every enterprise data entity has a named business owner accountable for its definition, quality, lifecycle and access, supported by named stewards. Ownership sits in the business, never in technology.
principles.rationale: Meridian currently has no single accountable owner for customer data, product data or the integration estate. Without ownership there is no one to arbitrate a definition, approve an access request, or accept the cost of poor quality — which is why quality problems have been pushed downstream to consumers and absorbed as manual effort. Ownership is also a precondition for the accountability that POPIA and the Joint Standards assume.
principles.implications:
1. A data ownership register must be established and maintained, with owners appointed by name and by role, not by department.
2. Data owners require the authority to refuse an access request and the budget to remediate quality in their own domain.
3. Definitional disputes are resolved by the owner, and the resolution is recorded in the business glossary.
4. Technology teams are custodians and operators of data; they are accountable for protecting it, not for defining it.
principles.measure: Proportion of Tier 1 data entities with a named, currently serving business owner. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Data is Protected and Purpose-Limited
principles.statement: Personal and sensitive data is collected for a stated lawful purpose, used only for purposes compatible with it, retained only as long as required, and protected in proportion to the harm its disclosure would cause.
principles.rationale: POPIA imposes consent, purpose limitation, data subject access and retention obligations, and Meridian must meet them across four disconnected customer masters — a materially harder problem than meeting them in one place. Insurance data is also inherently sensitive: health, financial position, family circumstance and claims history. The reputational and regulatory cost of mishandling it exceeds the cost of handling it properly.
principles.implications:
1. Purpose and lawful basis must be captured with the data at the point of collection and must travel with it into any copy.
2. Retention schedules must be enforced by systems, not by policy documents; data that cannot be deleted on schedule is a defect.
3. Data subject access and deletion requests must be servable across the whole estate — which is not possible without DP-02.
4. Classification drives control. Every data entity carries a classification, and controls are applied to that classification, not uniformly.
principles.measure: Median elapsed time to service a data subject access request across the full estate. Target: within the statutory period, without manual assembly.

principles.name: Data Lineage is Traceable
principles.statement: For any reported figure, it is possible to trace the data back through every transformation to its authoritative source, without manual reconstruction.
principles.rationale: IFRS 17 demands contract-level granularity that the legacy platforms currently supply only through manual reconciliation. Prudential Authority Guidance Notice G3/2025 signals that climate-related disclosure aligned to BCBS and IAIS practice is becoming mandatory, which imports the same lineage expectation into ESG reporting. Figures that cannot be traced cannot be defended to an auditor or a supervisor, and manual reconciliation is both a cost and a control weakness.
principles.implications:
1. Transformations must be declared and recorded in metadata, not embedded only in code or spreadsheets.
2. Spreadsheet-based reporting steps between a source system and a regulatory return must be identified and eliminated over time.
3. The enterprise data platform must capture lineage as a first-class output, not as documentation produced afterwards.
4. Lineage requirements apply to models and their inputs as well as to reports (see SP-03).
principles.owner: Chief Financial Officer / Chief Data Officer
principles.measure: Proportion of regulatory return line items with automated end-to-end lineage. Target: 90% by 2029.

principles.name: Reuse, then Buy, then Build
principles.statement: Capability is satisfied first by reusing an existing enterprise asset, then by acquiring a proven market solution, and only then by building. Building is a decision that must be justified, not a default.
principles.rationale: Meridian records 312 applications with uncertain completeness, several of which duplicate one another across lines of business. Duplication is the largest single contributor to a run cost that consumes 71% of the technology budget, and every additional bespoke asset adds permanently to that base. Building is warranted only where the capability is genuinely differentiating — which, for an insurer, is rarely the case in policy administration or general ledger and frequently the case in underwriting and pricing.
principles.implications:
1. A capability-to-application map must exist and be current, or reuse cannot be assessed.
2. Business cases must state what was considered for reuse and why it was rejected. 'Not investigated' is not a rejection.
3. Buying imports the vendor's data model and release cycle; those consequences are assessed at selection, not discovered later (see TP-01).
4. Where a bespoke build is approved, its total cost of ownership over the planning horizon must be stated and owned, not just its build cost.
principles.measure: Proportion of new solution decisions with a documented reuse assessment. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Capability is Exposed Through Managed Interfaces
principles.statement: Applications expose their capability and data through defined, versioned, documented interfaces. Direct access to another application's internal data store is not permitted.
principles.rationale: The estate carries roughly sixty point-to-point interfaces of mixed technology and no API gateway. Each one couples two systems at their internals, so that replacing either requires renegotiating every connection — which is a substantial part of why two core replacements failed. Managed interfaces are what make the incremental, reversible change required by BP-06 physically possible, and what allow the 1994 life platform to be wrapped rather than replaced in one step.
principles.implications:
1. An integration and API layer must be established, with a gateway, a catalogue and lifecycle management for interface versions.
2. Legacy systems that cannot expose modern interfaces are wrapped; the wrapper, not the legacy internals, becomes the contract.
3. Interfaces are products with owners, consumers, versions and deprecation notice periods, not project artifacts.
4. New point-to-point integration is a dispensation-level exception, not a design choice.
principles.measure: Proportion of inter-application traffic traversing the managed integration layer. Target: 80% by 2029. New point-to-point interfaces created: zero.

principles.name: Products are Configured, Not Coded
principles.statement: Insurance product definitions — cover, rating, rules, wordings, documents — are held as configuration maintained by the business, not as application code maintained by developers.
principles.rationale: Meridian takes nine to fourteen months to move a product from concept to market, principally because product configuration is hard-coded in the 1994 life platform. Affordability pressure and the sector-wide shift toward simpler products mean this cycle time is a commercial constraint, not just an inconvenience. Configuration also removes a release dependency between product change and system change, which is a resilience benefit as well as a speed one.
principles.implications:
1. Target policy administration platforms must be selected substantially on the strength of their product configuration capability.
2. Configuration is change and must be governed: versioned, tested, approved and auditable. 'Business maintained' does not mean ungoverned.
3. Product, actuarial and compliance staff require the skills and tooling to configure; this is a capability investment, not a system feature.
4. Legacy products may remain hard-coded. New and materially amended products may not.
principles.measure: Elapsed time from approved product concept to market. Target: under 90 days for a configuration-only product by 2029.

principles.name: Services are Channel-Agnostic
principles.statement: Business services are implemented once and consumed by every channel. Channels differ in presentation and journey, never in the underlying rule, price or record.
principles.rationale: Meridian reaches customers through tied agency, brokers, bancassurance, direct and digital, and emerging embedded partnerships. Each channel today has its own quotation path and its own record of the customer, which is the proximate cause of the four customer masters and a standing conduct risk: the same customer can receive different answers depending on how they approach the business. Channel-agnostic services are also the only economic way to add embedded partners at the pace the growth pillar assumes.
principles.implications:
1. Quotation, underwriting, policy issue, servicing and claims must be exposed as services, not embedded in channel applications.
2. Where a channel needs different behaviour, it must be expressed as configurable rule variation on the shared service, not as a separate implementation.
3. Retiring channel-specific duplicates is a migration cost that must be planned into the roadmap, not deferred indefinitely.
4. New channels — including embedded partners — must onboard by consuming existing services. A new channel is not a reason for a new stack.
principles.measure: Number of distinct implementations of quotation and policy issue across channels. Target: one per line of business by 2029.

principles.name: Usability and Accessibility
principles.statement: Applications are designed for the people who must actually use them — advisers, brokers, service staff and policyholders — including those with limited connectivity, limited data budgets, limited literacy or a disability.
principles.rationale: Meridian's funeral and life books are distributed heavily in township and rural markets where connectivity and data cost are real constraints, and the digital quote-to-issue completion rate of 31% indicates that current journeys lose two thirds of the people who begin them. Adviser productivity and broker retention are stated stakeholder concerns. A system that is technically correct and practically unusable delivers no capability.
principles.implications:
1. Customer-facing journeys must be designed and tested for low-bandwidth and low-end device conditions, not only for the office.
2. Accessibility standards must be adopted, stated in the standards catalogue and tested, not left to individual project judgement.
3. Usability is measured — completion rates, task times, error rates — and those measures are part of acceptance.
4. Internal-facing systems are held to the same standard as customer-facing ones; adviser productivity depends on it.
principles.measure: Digital quote-to-issue completion rate. Target: 60% by 2029.

principles.name: Technology Independence
principles.statement: Solutions are designed so that business capability and data are not permanently bound to a specific product, platform or supplier. The cost and route of exit are understood before entry.
principles.rationale: Meridian's most expensive constraint is a 1994 platform it cannot leave without also rebuilding everything that touches it. That is a lock-in problem, not a technology-age problem, and buying a modern product carelessly reproduces it. Independence is not vendor-neutrality for its own sake; it is the preservation of the enterprise's ability to change its mind at an acceptable cost.
principles.implications:
1. Every material platform selection must include a documented exit assessment: what it would cost and take to leave, and who holds the data.
2. Business logic is kept out of proprietary layers where a reasonable alternative exists.
3. Data must be extractable from any platform in a documented, non-proprietary form, and this must be contractually secured at procurement.
4. This principle is directional, not absolute. Deep use of a platform's native capability is often correct — but it is a decision to be taken knowingly and recorded (see GP-01).
principles.measure: Proportion of Tier 1 platforms with a current, reviewed exit assessment. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Controlled Diversity and Standards Conformance
principles.statement: The technology estate is deliberately constrained to a managed set of standards and products recorded in the Technology Standards Catalogue. Open and industry standards are preferred, and departures are approved rather than assumed.
principles.rationale: Uncontrolled diversity is a direct cost: every additional product carries licensing, skills, patching, monitoring and vendor management. With 71% of spend on run and no budget increase before FY2028, diversity that is not deliberately chosen is capacity taken from change. Standards conformance additionally supports interoperability, multi-vendor support and the supply-chain integration the embedded channels will require.
principles.implications:
1. A Technology Standards Catalogue must be established, with a lifecycle status for each entry — emerging, current, contained, retired.
2. A process for setting standards, reviewing them periodically and granting exceptions must exist. Standards without a review cycle become obstacles.
3. The existing platform inventory must be identified and documented before it can be constrained; the current 312-application figure is not trusted.
4. Constraint is not stasis. Deliberate experimentation with emerging technology is permitted within a contained status.
principles.measure: Proportion of the estate running on current-status standards. Target: 85% by 2029. Products outside the catalogue: trending to zero.

principles.name: Reduce the Cost of Run
principles.statement: Every architecture decision is assessed for its effect on the ongoing cost of operating the estate, and initiatives that add permanently to run cost must fund an offsetting reduction.
principles.rationale: Meridian2030 requires a cost-to-income ratio below 32% against a current 37.4%, and no increase in the technology budget is available before FY2028 — so change must be funded from run-cost reduction. A landscape where 71% of spend services the run cannot deliver a transformation agenda. Treating run cost as an outcome rather than a design input is how the estate reached this position.
principles.implications:
1. Decommissioning is part of the scope of any replacement initiative and is funded within it. A replacement that leaves the incumbent running has not been completed.
2. Total cost of ownership over the planning horizon, not implementation cost, is the basis for comparing options.
3. Technical debt must be recorded, sized and carried on a register, so that the cost of not acting is as visible as the cost of acting.
4. Automation of manual operational effort is a legitimate and prioritised architecture objective in its own right.
principles.owner: Chief Financial Officer / Chief Information Officer
principles.measure: Run-to-change spend ratio. Target: 60/40 by 2029. Applications decommissioned per year against those introduced.

principles.name: Resilience Proportionate to Criticality
principles.statement: Availability, recoverability and cyber resilience are engineered in proportion to the business criticality of the capability served, against tiers defined once and applied consistently.
principles.rationale: Joint Standard 2 of 2024 requires demonstrable cyber resilience and incident notification, and grid instability makes availability a live operational concern rather than a theoretical one. Uniform resilience is unaffordable; ad hoc resilience is unaccountable and cannot be evidenced to a supervisor. Tiering makes both the investment and the accepted residual risk explicit.
principles.implications:
1. A criticality tiering scheme must be defined and each capability assigned to a tier by its business owner.
2. Resilience targets are tested, and the evidence of testing is retained for supervisory purposes.
3. Where a capability's resilience is below its tier, the gap is recorded as accepted residual risk with a named accepting executive.
4. Third-party and cloud services are assessed against the tier of the capability they support, including their own concentration risk.
principles.owner: Chief Risk Officer / Chief Information Officer
principles.measure: Proportion of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capabilities meeting their stated resilience target under test. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Security is Built In
principles.statement: Security and privacy controls are designed into solutions from inception and are proportionate to the classification of the data and the criticality of the capability. Security is not a gate applied at the end.
principles.rationale: Joint Standard 2 of 2024 places cybersecurity and cyber resilience obligations on financial institutions with a determined notification template, and the FSCA has shown willingness to sanction individuals as well as firms. Insurance data is among the most sensitive an organisation can hold. Controls retrofitted after design are more expensive, less effective and frequently incomplete.
principles.implications:
1. Threat modelling is performed as part of solution design, not as a pre-release assessment.
2. Security architecture requirements are stated in the Architecture Requirements Specification alongside functional ones.
3. Security review has the authority to withhold approval, exercised through the same dispensation route as any other principle (GP-02).
4. Controls are proportionate. Applying maximum control uniformly is a failure of this principle, not an excess of compliance with it.
principles.measure: Proportion of material initiatives with a completed threat model before build commencement. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Least Privilege and Accountable Access
principles.statement: Access to data and function is granted at the minimum level required for a stated role, is attributable to an identified individual, and is reviewed on a defined cycle.
principles.rationale: Meridian's obligations under POPIA, FICA and the Joint Standards all assume the ability to say who did what to which record. Accumulated access — the historic pattern where permissions are added and never removed — is simultaneously a conduct risk, a fraud risk and a data protection failure. Claims leakage of four to six percent of short-term claims cost has an access-control dimension as well as a process one.
principles.implications:
1. Shared and generic accounts are not permitted for access to customer data. Where legacy platforms require them, the gap is registered and time-bound.
2. Role definitions are owned by the business, derived from the role catalogue, and reviewed at least annually.
3. Segregation of duties must be enforced by systems in the payment, claims settlement and policy alteration paths.
4. Privileged access is time-bound, justified and logged.
principles.measure: Proportion of access rights reviewed within the last 12 months. Target: 100%. Generic accounts with customer data access: zero.

principles.name: Models and Artificial Intelligence are Governed
principles.statement: Any model — actuarial, statistical or machine-learned — that influences a customer outcome, a price, an underwriting decision or a regulatory figure is registered, explainable, monitored, and has a named accountable owner.
principles.rationale: The FSCA and Prudential Authority published a joint report on artificial intelligence in November 2025 drawing on more than 2,100 responses across the financial sector, whose message was that adoption is rising fast and must be matched by accountability. Meridian has isolated AI pilots in claims triage with no model governance and no route to production. Under COFI, a model that produces an unfair outcome is a conduct failure regardless of how it was built, and an unexplainable model cannot be defended to a supervisor.
principles.implications:
1. A model register is required, covering scope, owner, training data, intended use, limitations and review cycle.
2. Models influencing customer outcomes must produce an explanation sufficient to justify the outcome to the customer and the regulator.
3. Model inputs are subject to the same lineage requirement as reported figures (DP-05).
4. Performance and bias are monitored in production on a defined cycle; a model that is not monitored must be withdrawn.
5. Vendor-supplied and embedded models are in scope. 'It came with the product' is not an exemption.
principles.measure: Proportion of production models influencing customer outcomes that are registered and monitored. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Architecture Decisions are Recorded and Traceable
principles.statement: Every significant architecture decision is recorded with its context, the options considered, the rationale for the choice, and the consequences accepted — and is traceable to the business driver it serves.
principles.rationale: Meridian has no repository, no decision record and no published principles, which means every architecture debate restarts from first principles and no one can reconstruct why the estate looks as it does. Recorded decisions are what convert a set of individual judgements into an institutional capability, and they are the evidence base that Joint Standard 1 of 2023 IT governance expects. They also allow a future team to distinguish a deliberate trade-off from an accident.
principles.implications:
1. An architecture decision record format must be adopted and its use made a condition of approval.
2. Decisions are held in the Architecture Repository, not in project documentation that is archived at closure.
3. A decision must name the principle or principles it engages, and where it departs from one, say so explicitly.
4. Superseding a decision requires a new record; decisions are amended by replacement, never edited silently.
principles.measure: Proportion of Architecture Board approvals with a corresponding decision record lodged in the repository. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Compliance is Assessed and Dispensations are Time-Bound
principles.statement: Conformance to these principles is formally assessed. Where a departure is justified, it is granted as an explicit dispensation with a stated expiry, a remediation plan and a named accepting executive.
principles.rationale: Principles without an assessment mechanism are advisory, and Meridian's history shows that advisory guidance does not survive delivery pressure. Equally, principles without a legitimate exception route drive non-compliance underground, which is worse than an approved departure. A time-bound dispensation makes the debt visible, dated and owned — which is the difference between a managed exception and accumulated technical debt.
principles.implications:
1. An architecture compliance review process must be defined, with entry criteria and materiality thresholds so that it scales.
2. A dispensation without an expiry date is not a dispensation; it is an unrecorded change to the principle.
3. Expiring dispensations are reported to the Architecture Board and feed the technical debt register under TP-03.
4. Repeated dispensations against the same principle are treated as evidence that the principle needs review, and are referred to Phase H.
principles.measure: Open dispensations past expiry. Target: zero. Compliance reviews completed against those required: 100%.

principles.name: Principles are Applied as a Set
principles.statement: These principles are interdependent and are applied together. Where two conflict, the higher precedence tier prevails; where they share a tier, the Architecture Board decides and records the reasoning.
principles.rationale: TOGAF is explicit that principles are inter-related and must be applied as a set, and that strict adherence to one may require a loose interpretation of another. Meridian's set contains deliberate tensions — accessibility against security, speed to market against fair-outcome evidence, technology independence against the benefit of a platform's native capability. Pretending these tensions do not exist produces either paralysis or arbitrary local resolution.
principles.implications:
1. Quoting a single principle in isolation to justify a decision is not sufficient; the decision must show the set was considered.
2. Known tensions are documented in the Principles Catalog and reviewed each ADM cycle rather than discovered anew each time.
3. Precedence tiers are assigned deliberately and changed only by the Architecture Board through the amendment process.
4. The rationale for a precedence decision is always recorded, because it becomes precedent.
principles.measure: Proportion of precedence decisions with a recorded rationale. Target: 100%.

principles.name: Security is Owned by the Business and Operated by Security
principles.statement: Accountability for a security risk sits with the business owner of the asset or process. The security function designs, advises and assures, but does not own the risk on the owner's behalf.
principles.rationale: A security function that owns every risk becomes the place risk goes to be forgotten. Joint Standard 1 of 2023 requires the governing body and senior management to own IT and cyber risk, not to delegate it into a technical team. Meridian's security function is sixty people against an establishment of 4,805; it cannot carry the enterprise's risk and should not be asked to.
principles.implications:
1. Every material security risk on the register names a business owner, not the CISO.
2. The CISO may block, but acceptance of a residual risk is signed by the accountable executive.
3. Security spend is proposed by the security function and approved against a business owner's risk appetite.
4. Escalation runs to the Risk Committee, and the CISO's line into it does not depend on Technology's agreement.
principles.measure: Every risk rated High or above on the security register names an accountable business owner outside the security function.

principles.name: Every Asset Has an Accountable Owner
principles.statement: Every application, data entity, interface and infrastructure component has a named owner accountable for its security posture. An asset with no owner is decommissioned or adopted; it is not left running.
principles.rationale: Controls cannot be applied to something nobody owns, and nothing unowned gets patched, reviewed or retired. Meridian has no data ownership register at all, roughly sixty interfaces of which forty-four are unmanaged, and a departmental reporting estate nobody has claimed since 2008. Each is a control gap that no amount of tooling closes.
principles.implications:
1. Ownership is recorded in the Architecture Repository, not in a spreadsheet held by security.
2. An unowned asset is raised as a finding with a date by which it is adopted or removed.
3. Ownership transfers explicitly on reorganisation; it does not lapse.
4. The owner is a named role, and the role is filled.
principles.measure: Every application and data entity in the repository resolves to a named owning role that is currently filled.

principles.name: Security Decisions are Risk-Based and Recorded
principles.statement: A control is applied because a stated risk justifies it, and the reasoning is recorded. Controls are not applied because they are conventional, and they are not omitted because they are inconvenient.
principles.rationale: Unrecorded security decisions are re-argued at every project and defended by whoever shouts loudest. Recording the risk, the options and the decision makes the position defensible to a supervisor and stops the same argument recurring. It also exposes controls that exist only because they always have.
principles.implications:
1. Every security exception carries a stated risk, an owner, an expiry and a remediation plan.
2. A control with no risk behind it is a candidate for removal, and removal is also a recorded decision.
3. Decision records use the enterprise format under GP-01; security does not keep a private one.
4. Aggregate exception exposure is reported to the Risk Committee quarterly.
principles.measure: Every open security exception has a recorded risk, a named accepting executive and an expiry date.

principles.name: Assurance is Independent of Delivery
principles.statement: The people who assure a control are not the people who built or operate it. Security testing, control testing and audit are structurally separated from delivery.
principles.rationale: Self-assessment reliably finds what it expects to find. Independence is what makes an assurance opinion worth reading, and it is what a supervisor looks for. Internal Audit already reports to the Audit Committee rather than to the Chief Risk Officer for exactly this reason.
principles.implications:
1. Penetration testing and control testing are commissioned outside the delivery team.
2. Security architecture review is separate from security engineering.
3. Findings are tracked to closure by the assurer, not by the party remediating them.
4. Where independence is not affordable for a small change, the departure is recorded.
principles.measure: No control assurance opinion in the last twelve months was issued by the team that built or operates the control.

principles.name: Every Action is Attributable to a Person
principles.statement: Every action taken against a Meridian system resolves to an individual human being. Shared, generic and service accounts are either eliminated or bound to a named accountable owner with brokered access.
principles.rationale: Attribution is the precondition for every other access control. Without it there is no investigation, no accountability and no defensible record for a supervisor or an ombud. Generic accounts persist on the mainframe for batch and support work, which means the platform carrying the largest book by policy count cannot fully answer who did what.
principles.implications:
1. Shared interactive accounts are removed. Where a service account is unavoidable it has a named owner and its credentials are brokered, not known.
2. Emergency access is available, individually attributed, time-limited and reviewed after use.
3. Logs record the human identity, not only the account.
4. Legacy platforms are remediated on a dated plan, not exempted indefinitely.
principles.measure: Zero shared interactive accounts in production; every service account has a named owner and brokered credentials.

principles.name: Access is Least Privilege and Time-Bounded
principles.statement: Access is granted at the minimum level a stated role requires, for a stated period, and expires unless renewed. Entitlement does not accumulate with tenure.
principles.rationale: Privilege creep is the quiet failure mode of long-serving staff: an eighteen-year underwriter accumulates access nobody has revisited. Time-bounding turns access review from an annual archaeology exercise into an expiry event, which is both cheaper and more reliable.
principles.implications:
1. Access is requested against a role, not copied from a colleague.
2. Every grant has an expiry. Permanent access is a recorded exception, not a default.
3. Role definitions are owned by the business, reviewed annually, and reconciled against actual entitlement.
4. A change of role removes the old entitlement before granting the new.
principles.measure: Access review completed within the last twelve months for every system holding Confidential or Restricted data, with no entitlement older than its expiry.

principles.name: Privileged Access is Brokered, Never Standing
principles.statement: Administrative and privileged access is requested, approved, time-boxed and recorded at the moment of use. Nobody holds standing privilege.
principles.rationale: Standing privilege is the single largest amplifier of a compromised credential: it converts one phished account into an estate-wide event. Brokering costs a few seconds per session and removes the amplifier. It also produces, as a by-product, the audit record that Joint Standard 2 expects.
principles.implications:
1. Privileged sessions are requested against a stated task and approved by someone other than the requester.
2. Sessions are time-boxed and recorded, and the recording is retained.
3. Break-glass access exists, is monitored in real time, and triggers a review every time it is used.
4. Vendors and contractors obtain privilege through the same broker as employees.
principles.measure: No standing privileged entitlement in production; every privileged session in the period traces to an approved, time-boxed request.

principles.name: Trust is Verified, Not Inferred from Location
principles.statement: Being on the corporate network confers no trust. Every request is authenticated and authorised on its own merits, whatever its origin.
principles.rationale: The perimeter stopped describing Meridian's estate some time ago: forty-six branches, two contact centres, a cloud region, a bancassurance integration and 3,400 brokerages all sit inside or across it. A control model that grants trust by network position grants it to whoever reaches the network.
principles.implications:
1. Internal service-to-service calls authenticate. Network position is not an authentication factor.
2. Multi-factor authentication applies to remote and privileged access, and to any access to Restricted data.
3. Segmentation remains valuable for containment, but is not relied on for authorisation.
4. Legacy protocols that cannot authenticate are wrapped or replaced on a dated plan.
principles.measure: Every new service-to-service integration authenticates independently of network position.

principles.name: Data is Classified Before It is Protected
principles.statement: Every data entity carries a classification, and the classification determines the controls. Protection is proportionate to classification, not to the preferences of the system that happens to hold the data.
principles.rationale: Uniform controls over-protect public data and under-protect restricted data at the same time, and cost more than either. Meridian holds health data for underwriting, financial data for claims and identity data for FICA, all in the same estate. Without classification the controls cannot be proportionate, and the POPIA obligation cannot be evidenced.
principles.implications:
1. Classification is an attribute of the data entity, not of the application, and it travels with copies.
2. The control set per classification is defined once, in the standard, and applied consistently.
3. Unclassified data is treated as Confidential until classified.
4. Reclassification is a recorded decision with an owner.
principles.measure: Every data entity in the repository carries a classification, and every store holding Restricted data meets the Restricted control set.

principles.name: Personal Data Carries Its Purpose
principles.statement: Personal data is collected for a stated lawful purpose, and that purpose travels with every copy. Data collected for one purpose is not repurposed without a fresh basis.
principles.rationale: POPIA's purpose limitation is not satisfiable by a policy document; it has to be enforceable at the point of use. Meridian holds roughly 1.9 million policyholders across four customer masters with no common identifier, which means a consent withdrawal cannot currently be propagated with confidence. That is a compliance exposure and an operational one.
principles.implications:
1. Lawful basis and consent state are captured at collection and propagated with every copy.
2. A withdrawal of consent propagates to every copy within the statutory period.
3. Analytical and model use of personal data is checked against the recorded purpose before processing.
4. Retention is enforced by the system against the purpose, not by a schedule nobody executes.
principles.measure: A consent withdrawal applied to any customer propagates to every store holding that customer's data within the statutory period.

principles.name: Encryption is the Default, Not the Exception
principles.statement: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest by default. Not encrypting is the decision that requires justification.
principles.rationale: Inverting the default removes the most common failure, which is that encryption was simply never considered. It also simplifies assurance: the question becomes which stores are exceptions rather than which are protected. Key management, not the cipher, is where this principle actually bites.
principles.implications:
1. Keys are managed centrally, rotated on a schedule, and never held by the application that uses them.
2. Unencrypted stores are exceptions with an owner, an expiry and a remediation plan.
3. Encryption does not substitute for access control; a decrypted read by an over-privileged account is still a breach.
4. Legacy datasets that cannot be encrypted in place are scheduled for migration, not exempted.
principles.measure: Every store holding Confidential or Restricted data is encrypted at rest, or holds a current exception with an expiry.

principles.name: Production Data Does Not Leave Production
principles.statement: Personal and financial data does not appear in test, development or analytical environments in identifiable form. Non-production environments use synthetic or irreversibly masked data.
principles.rationale: Non-production environments carry production data with a fraction of production's controls, and they are where breaches quietly originate. The objection is always that realistic testing needs real data; the answer is that masked data preserves shape and distribution, and that the objection is usually about effort rather than realism.
principles.implications:
1. Masking or synthesis happens at extraction, not after loading.
2. A defect requiring production data is investigated in production, under brokered privileged access.
3. Extracts to analysts are governed by the same classification and purpose rules as any other copy.
4. Where masking is genuinely infeasible, the environment is controlled to production standard.
principles.measure: No identifiable personal data present in any non-production environment, evidenced by scan.

principles.name: Threat Models Precede Build
principles.statement: Every material change has a threat model completed and reviewed before build begins, proportionate to the change.
principles.rationale: Controls designed after the fact are more expensive, less effective and frequently bolted to the wrong place. A threat model is cheap at design time and reveals the assumptions that a control review never reaches. Meridian currently completes one for 23% of material initiatives, and the Meridian 2030 objective is 100% by 2027.
principles.implications:
1. Threat modelling is a gate in the delivery process, not an artifact produced at the end for audit.
2. Proportionality is defined: a new external interface is modelled, a copy change is not.
3. The model names the assets, the actors, the trust boundaries and the assumptions.
4. Findings become requirements in the same backlog as functional work, not a separate security list.
principles.measure: Threat model completed and reviewed before build for 100% of material initiatives.

principles.name: Interfaces are Authenticated, Authorised and Logged
principles.statement: Every interface between components authenticates its caller, authorises the specific request, and logs the outcome. No component reads another's data store directly.
principles.rationale: The integration estate is where security assumptions go unexamined. Meridian has roughly sixty point-to-point interfaces, forty-four of them unmanaged, and four that read another application's database directly. A direct database read bypasses every control the owning application implements, and leaves no record that it happened.
principles.implications:
1. Direct database reads between applications are eliminated, not documented.
2. Interfaces are catalogued, versioned and owned. An uncatalogued interface is a finding.
3. Authorisation is per request and per resource, not per connection.
4. Interface logs are retained and reach the SIEM.
principles.measure: Zero direct database reads between applications; every interface in the catalogue authenticates and logs.

principles.name: Secrets are Managed, Never Embedded
principles.statement: Credentials, keys and tokens are held in a managed secret store and retrieved at runtime. They do not appear in source, configuration, scripts or documentation.
principles.rationale: Embedded secrets survive everything: repository history, backups, handover documents and the memory of everyone who has seen them. They cannot be rotated in any meaningful sense, and they turn a source-code exposure into a production compromise.
principles.implications:
1. Secrets are retrieved at runtime from a managed store, with access attributed and logged.
2. Rotation is automated and does not require a code change or a release.
3. Source and configuration are scanned for secrets on every commit.
4. A secret that has been exposed is treated as compromised and rotated, whether or not use is suspected.
principles.measure: Zero secrets detected in source, configuration or scripts on scan; rotation completed on schedule.

principles.name: Security Controls are Testable and Tested
principles.statement: A control that cannot be tested is not a control. Every control has a stated test, and the test is executed on a defined cycle.
principles.rationale: Untested controls fail silently and are discovered during an incident, which is the most expensive possible moment. Requiring testability at design time also improves the design: a control nobody can describe a test for is usually vague rather than strong.
principles.implications:
1. Every control names its test and its cycle at the point it is designed.
2. Test results are recorded and failures raise a finding with an owner and a date.
3. Controls inherited from a supplier are tested or independently attested; assurance is not assumed.
4. Detection controls are tested by simulating the event they are meant to detect.
principles.measure: Every control rated Key has a documented test executed within its stated cycle.

principles.name: Assume Compromise
principles.statement: The architecture assumes that prevention will sometimes fail. Blast radius, containment and recovery are designed for, not left to incident response to improvise.
principles.rationale: Designing only for prevention produces an estate that is brittle precisely where it matters: everything holds until one control fails, and then nothing does. Assuming compromise changes design decisions — segmentation, privilege, logging and recovery all become architectural rather than operational concerns.
principles.implications:
1. A design states what an attacker reaches if a given component is compromised.
2. Segmentation limits lateral movement, and the limit is tested.
3. Critical data has an immutable, offline-recoverable copy.
4. Incident response is exercised against the architecture, not only against a runbook.
principles.measure: Every Tier 1 application has a documented blast-radius assessment reviewed within twelve months.

principles.name: Detection is Designed In, Not Bolted On
principles.statement: Systems emit the telemetry required to detect misuse, and they emit it by design. Detection requirements are stated at design time alongside functional requirements.
principles.rationale: Retrofitting telemetry is expensive and usually incomplete, because the events worth detecting are known to the designer and not to the person instrumenting afterwards. Joint Standard 2 of 2024 expects detection and notification within a determined timeframe, which is not achievable if the signal was never emitted.
principles.implications:
1. Every design states the events it emits and why they matter.
2. Telemetry reaches the SIEM within a stated latency, and gaps are findings.
3. Detection use cases are owned, tested and retired when they stop earning their place.
4. Logging respects classification: telemetry does not become an unprotected copy of restricted data.
principles.measure: Every Tier 1 application emits the telemetry named in the logging standard, and it reaches the SIEM.

principles.name: Recovery is Proven, Not Documented
principles.statement: Recovery objectives are met in a test, not asserted in a plan. An untested recovery capability is assumed absent.
principles.rationale: Recovery plans that have never been executed fail on first use, and they fail during the incident. Meridian has tested recovery for 41% of Tier 1 capabilities; the remainder are documented and unproven, which for planning purposes means they do not exist.
principles.implications:
1. Every Tier 1 capability tests recovery against its stated objective at least annually.
2. A failed test is a finding with an owner and a date, not an input to a revised objective.
3. Recovery from a destructive event, including ransomware, is tested distinctly from recovery from failure.
4. Test evidence is retained and available to the supervisor.
principles.measure: 100% of Tier 1 capabilities meet a tested recovery time and recovery point objective within twelve months.

principles.name: A Third Party's Security is Meridian's Accountability
principles.statement: Work may be outsourced; accountability may not. A supplier's control environment is assessed, evidenced and monitored to the standard Meridian would apply to itself.
principles.rationale: Joint Standard 2 of 2024 places third-party and concentration risk with the institution, not the supplier. Meridian's operating model runs through a bancassurance bank, 3,400 brokerages, 280 repairers, platform vendors and a cloud provider. A control failure at any of them is Meridian's incident, and the supervisor will treat it as such.
principles.implications:
1. Security requirements are in the contract before signature, including notification obligations and audit rights.
2. Assurance is evidenced, whether by independent attestation or by Meridian's own testing, and refreshed.
3. Third-party access follows the same identity, privilege and logging principles as internal access.
4. Concentration is monitored: several critical dependencies on one supplier is itself a risk.
principles.measure: Every Critical third party has current security assurance evidence and a contractual notification obligation.

principles.name: Software Provenance is Known
principles.statement: Meridian knows what its software is made of. Components, their origin and their known vulnerabilities are recorded and monitored for every system in production.
principles.rationale: Most of the code running in the estate was not written by Meridian. Without an inventory of components, a disclosed vulnerability turns into a manual search across an estate nobody has catalogued, which is exactly when speed matters most.
principles.implications:
1. A software bill of materials is produced at build and retained for every deployed system.
2. Components are checked against vulnerability feeds continuously, not at release.
3. Remediation timescales are set by severity and exposure, and tracked to closure.
4. Vendors supply provenance for their components, or the gap is recorded as an accepted risk.
principles.measure: A current software bill of materials exists for every Tier 1 application in production.

principles.name: Exit is Designed at Entry
principles.statement: How Meridian leaves a supplier, and how its data is returned or destroyed, is agreed before the relationship starts.
principles.rationale: Exit terms negotiated at the end are negotiated from weakness, and data held by a departing supplier is the most common loose end. Designing exit at entry is cheap; discovering at exit that there is no extraction path is not. This is a directional principle: cost and reuse may reasonably outweigh it, provided the departure is recorded.
principles.implications:
1. Data extraction format, timescale and destruction evidence are agreed in the contract.
2. Exit cost is assessed at selection and recorded alongside the decision.
3. Where a supplier cannot meet exit requirements, the residual risk is accepted by a named executive.
4. Exit provisions are revisited at renewal, not left to run unchanged.
principles.measure: Every new supplier contract holding Meridian data states extraction format, timescale and destruction evidence.
